food-webs.description: An energy pyramid is a presentation of the trophic levels in an ecosystem. Energy from the sun is transferred through the ecosystem by passing through various trophic levels. Roughly 10% of the energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next, thus preventing large amounts of trophic levels. There must be higher amounts of biomass at the bottom of the pyramid to support the energy and biomass requirements of the higher trophic levels.

homeostasis.description: Hebrew-labeled sorting of various animal groups into the different thermoregulation categories (poikiloterms, homeotherms, ectotherms, endotherms). This diagram demonstrates the fact that the "thermal steadiness" categories (homeotherms - steady temperature, marked by a smooth color background at the bottom half, vs. poikilotherms - varying temperature, marked by a zig-zag pattern at the top half), do not overlap with the "thermal control" categories (ectotherms - externally controlled, marked by the blue background at the right half, vs. endotherms - internally controlled, marked by the red background at the left half). Based on a similar diagram appearing in Encyclopedia of Ecology by Brian D. Fath, p. 3511. To place this image in a wiki page and activate the four words surrounding the circle into links to the corresponding hewiki articles, use the following code, generated using the ImageMapEdit tool: <imagemap> File:Biological_thermoregulation_categories,_Hebrew.svg|300px| rect 168 511 398 548 [[w:he:הומיאותרמיות]] rect 160 17 406 61 [[w:he:פויקילותרמיות]] rect 510 171 551 393 [[w:he:בעלי דם קר]] rect 16 180 52 386 [[w:he:בעלי דם חם]] circle 280 285 222 [[#/media/File:Biological_thermoregulation_categories,_Hebrew.svg]] desc none </imagemap>

kinetic-energy.commonsTitle: File:Diagram comparing kinetic energy applicable to conventional and high-speed trains.png
kinetic-energy.description: The diagram compares the kinetic energy applicable to conventional and high-speed trains respectively. The upper diagram shows that a conventional, low-speed train travelling at 100 kilometres per hour (62 miles per hour), cutting off its power at the foot of a hill about 40 metres (about 130 feet) high, and "coasting" up the grade will come to a stop at the summit – i.e., it loses 100 km/h in the process. The lower diagram poses the same criteria applied to a high-speed train travelling at 350 km/h (about 220 mph) before it cuts off power and coasts up the hill. It will pass the summit at 335 km/h (208 mph) – i.e., it loses only 15 km/h (9 mph) in the process. The source of this phenomenon is kinetic energy, a principle of classical mechanics: it is equal to half the product of the mass and the square of the speed. In formula form: Ek=12mv2 where m is the mass and v is the speed (magnitude of the velocity) of the body. Kinetic energy increases in proportion to the square of the speed: doubling the speed, for example, increases the kinetic energy four times. This phenomenon is important for train performance since it allows high-speed trains to climb much steeper gradients (as steep as 5%, 1 in 20) compared with a 2.5% maximum for conventional trains. It is the reason why track must be as straight as possible to allow maximum utilisation of kinetic energy without being forced to waste it by braking. A side benefit is that earthwork costs on high-speed lines are lower than on conventional lines because the quantities of earth and rock needing to be moved in cut-and-fill earthworks are smaller. Source: VFT Joint Venture (1990). VFT Project Evaluation Report. Canberra. Ch. 4, Performance criteria. p. 2.

astronomy.commonsTitle: File:The Future Physics of Planet Earth (40217810733).jpg
astronomy.description: Designed by Danny Hillis, this solid metal prototype cam just arrived from the Long Now Foundation. She has a lovely, lithe and sinuous shape that emerges from the precise encoding of a fundamental future for Earth’s next 10,000 years. In the design of a clock that will run for 10,000 years, the Long Now Foundation decided to use the passage of the sun as a feedback loop on the precision of the mechanical mechanism. Every year, the timing of the sun varies with the seasons; the solar clock repeats an annual pattern as the Earth, with its tilted axis of rotation, circles the Sun. But over thousands of years, it changes in two major ways: 1) the Earth’s rotation slows by 1.8 msec/day, and this adds up to a 16 hour error over 10,000 years. 2) the axis of rotation itself wobbles over a 26,000 cycle. In 8,000 years, we will have a new North Star — Deneb instead of Polaris. So, the cam encodes both, the steady lengthening of the day and the cyclical shift of Earth’s axial angle. Here is a <a href="http://blog.longnow.org/02018/12/05/the-equation-of-time-cam-keeping-good-time-for-10000-years" rel="noreferrer nofollow">writeup</a> with more details and diagrams of the curves: “The equation of time cam is a piece of the clock that converts solar noon to absolute noon. The cam represents 12,000 years of this equation, with one rotation per year. While the Clock’s day to day time-keeper is a slow pendulum, a solar synchronizer and cam like this one are needed to correct drift over the long haul. On any sunny day, when the sun lines up with this mechanism, light is focused onto a piece of nickel-titanium wire that reacts when heated by the sun. This motion is used to synchronize the Clock to solar noon. The synchronization is also modified slightly by the equation of time cam, which accounts for the +/- 15 minute difference of solar to absolute time. Due to meteor impacts and volcanic eruptions, the clock may not see the sun for several years, so it must be accurate enough to stay within the range of this correction during those times.”
